resources.title: AQA pseudo-code
resources.summary: The pseudo-code AQA uses in every Computer Science paper, on one page: assignment, operators, selection, loops, arrays, records, subroutines, strings, conversion and input and output, each with an example.
resources.statusNote: You read this style in the exam. Each question says what form the answer must take: pseudo-code, program code or a flowchart. Where pseudo-code is allowed, you may use this style or any style of your own that is clear, consistent and unambiguous. Where program code is asked for, write in the language you learnt at school. AQA says its guide "is not confidential and can be freely shared with students", and it is linked below.

blocks.body: **Indexing starts at 0**, for arrays and strings alike, unless a question says otherwise. Keywords are in capitals, and a constant's name is written in capitals too.

blocks.title: Selection and loops
rows: also `ELSE IF` for more than two branches
runs at least once; stops when the condition is True
may run no times; runs while the condition is True
gives 1, 3, 5; with no STEP it goes up in 1s; a negative STEP counts down, so `5 TO 1 STEP -2` gives 5, 3, 1
once for each character of a string, or item of an array

blocks.title: Arrays, records and subroutines
rows: with `table ← [[1, 2], [2, 4], [3, 6], [4, 8]]`, `table[3][1]` is 8: the fourth list, then its second item

blocks.body:
**A record, written out.**

```
RECORD Car
   make : String
   model : String
   price : Real
ENDRECORD
myCar ← Car('Ford', 'Focus', 1399.99)
myCar.model ← 'Fiesta'
OUTPUT myCar.model
```

This outputs Fiesta. The record lists the fields and their types, `Car(...)` makes one car, and a full stop picks out one field.

**A function, written out.**

```
SUBROUTINE add(a, b)
   result ← a + b
   RETURN result
ENDSUBROUTINE
answer ← add(2, 3)
```

`answer` is 5. `RETURN` sends the value back to the line that called the subroutine.

**Tracing a loop.** Write down each variable every time round.

```
total ← 0
FOR i ← 1 TO 5 STEP 2
   total ← total + i
ENDFOR
OUTPUT total
```

When `i` is 1, `total` becomes 1. When `i` is 3, `total` becomes 4. When `i` is 5, `total` becomes 9. The output is 9.

applications.title: Planning a program before typing it
applications.body: Programmers sketch the logic in pseudo-code first, because it can be read and checked by anyone, whatever language the program ends up in.

applications.title: One exam style, whatever language you learnt
applications.body: AQA supports three languages, C#, Python and VB.NET, so its questions show algorithms in pseudo-code that every student can read. A question might show a linear search and ask what it outputs. Reading it is the same skill as reading Python, with different spelling.

resources.title: Logic gates
resources.summary: The four gates in the specification, NOT, AND, OR and XOR: each symbol with its truth table, the Boolean expression for it, and how they join into circuits.

visual.alt: A NOT gate drawn as a triangle with a small circle at its tip, input A and output Q, with a truth table showing the output is the opposite of the input

blocks.caption: **NOT** turns 1 into 0 and 0 into 1. Written with a bar over the letter: $Q = \overline{A}$.

visual.alt: An AND gate drawn as a D shape with inputs A and B and output Q, with a truth table showing the output is 1 only when both inputs are 1

blocks.caption: **AND** gives 1 only when **both** inputs are 1. Written with a dot: $Q = A \,.\, B$.

visual.alt: An OR gate drawn as a curved shield shape with inputs A and B and output Q, with a truth table showing the output is 1 when either input is 1

blocks.caption: **OR** gives 1 when **either or both** inputs are 1. Written with a plus: $Q = A + B$.

visual.alt: An XOR gate drawn as an OR shape with an extra curved line at its inputs, inputs A and B and output Q, with a truth table showing the output is 1 when exactly one input is 1

blocks.caption: **XOR**, short for exclusive or, is written with a circled plus, $Q = A \oplus B$, and gives 1 when **exactly one** input is 1. When both are 1 it gives 0, which is where it differs from OR.

blocks.body: **Putting them together.** $(A \text{ AND } B) \text{ OR } (\text{NOT } C)$ is written $(A \,.\, B) + \overline{C}$. A truth table for three inputs has $2^3 = 8$ rows. The specification uses only these four gates: no NAND or NOR.

applications.title: A car's interior light
applications.body: The light comes on if the driver's door OR the passenger's door is open: an OR gate, with each door switch as an input.

applications.title: Two-hand safety
applications.body: A factory press only moves if both of the operator's hands are on their buttons: an AND gate, so neither hand can be under it.

applications.title: Adding in binary
applications.body: Inside every processor, an XOR gate gives the sum digit of two bits and an AND gate the carry: $1 + 1$ is $0$ carry $1$.

resources.title: Number bases and ASCII
resources.summary: Decimal, binary and hexadecimal side by side from 0 to 15, the place values to convert up to 255, and the ASCII codes for capital letters, lower case letters and digits.

blocks.title: 0 to 15 in each base
blocks.note: Decimal is base 10, the everyday system. Some books call it denary; AQA's papers say decimal. One hexadecimal digit is exactly four binary digits, a nibble. That is why hex is used: $1010\,1111$ is $\text{AF}$, far easier to read and copy.

blocks.title: Binary place values, for a byte
blocks.note: Add the place values under each 1: $128 + 32 + 16 + 4 = 180$. The largest byte is $1111\,1111 = 255 = \text{FF}$.

blocks.body:
**Decimal to binary, in steps.** Take 180. Go along the place values from 128 and ask each time: does it fit into what is left?

128 fits: write 1, and 52 is left. 64 does not fit: write 0. 32 fits: write 1, and 20 is left. 16 fits: write 1, and 4 is left. 8 does not fit: write 0. 4 fits: write 1, and 0 is left. 2 and 1 do not fit: write 0 and 0.

So 180 is $1011\,0100$.

**Binary to hexadecimal.** Split the byte into two halves of four bits: $1011$ and $0100$. From the first table, $1011$ is B and $0100$ is 4, so the answer is $\text{B4}$.

**Hexadecimal to decimal.** The left digit counts 16s and the right digit counts 1s. B is 11, so $\text{B4}$ is $11 \times 16 + 4 = 180$.

blocks.title: ASCII codes that run in sequence
rows: `b` 98 … `z` 122: each is 32 more than its capital
blocks.note: 7-bit ASCII has 128 codes, 0 to 127, which is enough for English and little else. Unicode uses the same codes up to 127 and then carries on, so it can hold many alphabets and special symbols, a far greater range of characters.

applications.title: Colours on a web page
applications.body: A colour such as #FF8800 is three bytes in hexadecimal: red FF (255), green 88 (136) and blue 00 (0). Designers type the hex because six digits are shorter than 24 bits.

applications.title: Sorting names
applications.body: A computer sorts text by comparing character codes. Because capitals come before lower case in ASCII, a simple sort puts "Zoe" before "adam".

resources.title: Units of storage
resources.summary: Bits, nibbles and bytes, and the decimal prefixes from kilobyte to terabyte, with how to convert between them and how to work out a file size.

blocks.title: From bits to terabytes
rows: 4 bits, half a byte (useful for hexadecimal, not named in the specification)
blocks.note: AQA uses the **decimal** prefixes, powers of 1,000. You may see 1,024 elsewhere; for the exam, use 1,000.

blocks.body:
**Converting.** Going to a bigger unit, divide by 1,000 (or by 8 from bits to bytes). Going to a smaller one, multiply.

**File sizes.** An image: $\text{width} \times \text{height} \times \text{colour depth}$ bits. Width and height are counted in pixels, and colour depth is the number of bits used for each pixel. A sound: $\text{sampling rate} \times \text{sample resolution} \times \text{seconds}$ bits. The sampling rate is the number of samples taken each second, and the sample resolution is the number of bits in each sample. Divide by 8 for bytes.

**An image.** 1,000 pixels by 800 pixels at 24 bits a pixel is $1{,}000 \times 800 \times 24 = 19{,}200{,}000$ bits. Divide by 8: $2{,}400{,}000$ bytes. Divide by 1,000: $2{,}400$ kB. Divide by 1,000 again: $2.4$ MB.

**A sound.** 10 seconds at 8,000 samples a second and 16 bits a sample is $8{,}000 \times 16 \times 10 = 1{,}280{,}000$ bits. Divide by 8: $160{,}000$ bytes, which is $160$ kB.

applications.title: Choosing a phone
applications.body: A phone with 128 GB, which is 128,000 MB, holds about $128{,}000 \div 2.4 \approx 53{,}000$ photos of the size worked out above, before any compression.

applications.title: Download times
applications.body: Broadband is sold in megabits per second, not megabytes. A 40 Mb/s line moves at most $40 \div 8 = 5$ MB each second.
